a: He got up and left that place
t: Into Judea and across the Jordan
p: Jesus leaves Galilee for the last time. From here on, Mark's story moves toward Jerusalem.
b: This is Jesus' last departure from Galilee in Mark. "The far side of the Jordan" is Perea, the land east of the river ruled, like Galilee, by Herod Antipas. Pilgrims from Galilee often went south on that side of the river and crossed back near Jericho (10:46), avoiding Samaria. Mark's wording is loose ("Judea and the far side of the Jordan"), and later copyists smoothed it in two different ways (see the variant). Matthew has the same journey in Matthew 19:1. The whole section 8:27–10:52 takes place "on the road" (8:27; 9:33; 10:17, 32, 52), and this verse starts its last stage.

p: In Mark the question is whether divorce is allowed at all, perhaps asked in Herod Antipas' territory.
b: In Matthew the Pharisees ask whether a man may divorce "on any ground at all" (Matthew 19:3), a question from the debate between the schools of Hillel and Shammai (see the note there). Mark's question is broader: may a man divorce at all? Every Jewish teacher of the time would have said yes, since Deuteronomy 24:1–4 assumes it, so the question tests whether Jesus will openly set himself against Moses. It was also dangerous ground. Mark does not say where the debate took place, but Jesus may be in the land of Herod Antipas (Perea, beyond the Jordan; see 10:1), who had divorced his first wife to marry Herodias, and Mark has already told how John the Baptist was killed for condemning that marriage (6:17–29).

a: Moses let a man write out a divorce document
p: Jesus asks what Moses "commanded"; the Pharisees answer that Moses "let" a man divorce.
b: Mark sets the two verbs against each other. Jesus asks what Moses "commanded" (ἐνετείλατο); the Pharisees answer that Moses "permitted" (ἐπέτρεψεν) a divorce document. Deuteronomy 24:1 does not command divorce. It assumes that men divorce, and rules that the man must give the woman a written release: "He writes her a certificate of divorce, puts it in her hand, and sends her away from his house" (Deuteronomy 24:1). The document protected her, because it let her marry again. In Matthew the roles are reversed: the Pharisees speak of Moses' order and Jesus of his permission (Matthew 19:7–8). Scholars use the difference in the debate over which Gospel was written first.

p: The same hardness Mark finds in Jesus' opponents (3:5) and in his own disciples (6:52; 8:17).
b: The Greek word, sklērokardia, comes from the Greek Old Testament, where Moses tells Israel to "circumcise" their hard hearts (Deuteronomy 10:16 in the Septuagint; compare Jeremiah 4:4). The law on divorce, Jesus says, was a concession to people who would not be taught, not a picture of what God wants. Mark uses the idea of the hard heart for Jesus' opponents (3:5) and, more surprisingly, for the Twelve (6:52; 8:17). The point is not that Jews in particular are hard-hearted: Mark applies it to everyone, the disciples first.

p: Jesus answers a law about divorce by going back to the creation of man and woman.
b: Jesus quotes Genesis 1:27 in its Greek form, "male and female he made them"; this site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads "male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). Then he joins it to Genesis 2:24 (10:7–8). His argument is that God's purpose "from the start of creation" stands above a later concession. A Jewish rule book of the same period, the Damascus Document linked to the Qumran community, uses the same verse against a man taking a second wife (CD 4:20–5:2), so the move was not unheard of among Jews. Mark does not name the subject; "he made them" means God, and later copyists added the word (see the variant).

a: the two will become one flesh
p: Jesus follows the Greek Old Testament, which adds "the two" to Genesis 2:24.
b: This site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads "they become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). The Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, has "the two will become one flesh," and Jesus' words follow it, as do Paul's (1 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 5:31). Jesus draws the conclusion himself: "no longer two, but one flesh." A marriage, in this reading, is not only a contract that can be undone but a new unit God has made. See the note on Matthew 19:5.

a: When they had gone into the house
p: Mark often has Jesus explain things to the disciples privately, "in the house."
b: This is a pattern in Mark: Jesus teaches the crowd or answers opponents in public, then explains further to the disciples in private, often "in the house" (4:10, 34; 7:17; 9:28, 33). Literary critics see Mark's own church in this picture: the house was where his readers met, and the private explanation is the teaching meant for them. Here the private saying (10:11–12) is sharper than the public one, and its second half (10:12) speaks to a world where wives could divorce husbands.

a: Anyone who divorces his wife and marries someone else
p: Mark, Luke and Paul give the saying without Matthew's "except for sexual sin."
b: Mark's form of the saying has no exception. So does Luke's (Luke 16:18), and Paul gives it as a command of the Lord with no exception (1 Corinthians 7:10–11), though he then allows a believer to let an unbelieving spouse leave (1 Corinthians 7:15). Matthew twice adds "except for sexual sin" (Matthew 5:32; 19:9). Most scholars think Mark's short form is closer to what Jesus said, and that Matthew spells out an exception that Jewish hearers would have taken for granted, since adultery was thought to end a marriage. Others think Matthew adds a real change. Churches still differ on remarriage after divorce: see the cards on Matthew 5:32 and Matthew 19:3–12.

p: Jesus makes the husband guilty of adultery against his own wife, something Jewish law did not say.
b: In the law of Moses and in the ancient world generally, adultery was a wrong against a husband: a man committed adultery by having sex with another man's wife, and a married woman by having sex with any man not her husband. A husband could not commit adultery against his own wife. Jesus' phrase "against her" treats the wife as the one wronged, which puts husband and wife on the same footing. A few scholars read "against her" as "with her," meaning the second wife, but the first wife is the usual reading. Matthew and Luke leave the phrase out.

a: if she herself divorces her husband
t: A wife who divorces her husband
p: Jewish law gave only the husband the right to divorce; Roman law let either partner end a marriage.
b: Under the law of Moses as it was read in Jesus' time, only a husband could divorce. A wife could at most ask a court to make him do it. Josephus says that when Herod's sister Salome sent her husband a bill of divorce, she acted "not according to the Jewish laws" (Antiquities 15.259–260), and that Herodias "parted from a living husband" to marry Antipas (Antiquities 18.136). Under Roman law, and in many Greek cities, either partner could end a marriage. So 10:12 speaks to Mark's readers in the Roman world, whether as Mark's application of Jesus' teaching or, as some argue, as Jesus' own jab at Herodias. Some evidence suggests Jewish women did sometimes initiate divorce: Jewish marriage contracts from Elephantine in Egypt (400s BC) allow it, and Tal Ilan argued that a papyrus from the Judean Desert (XHev/Se 13) is a divorce written by a wife, though others read it differently.

p: Only here do the Gospels say Jesus was indignant. Matthew and Luke leave the word out.
b: The verb aganakteō means to be indignant or annoyed. Mark uses it of the disciples (10:41; 14:4), but only here of Jesus. (The Plain English Translation says "grew angry" here and at 14:4, and "annoyed" at 10:41, as in Matthew 20:24; the Greek verb is the same.) Matthew and Luke drop it from this story (Matthew 19:14; Luke 18:16). Mark's Jesus has strong feelings: anger and grief (3:5), compassion (6:34), indignation (here), love (10:21). Scholars who hold that Mark wrote first count this among the places where the later Gospels softened Mark's picture of Jesus.

a: The kingdom of God is for people like them
p: The kingdom belongs to those who receive it as a gift, as children do. Churches have read this about baptism too.
b: Children in the ancient world had no status, no claims and nothing to give. The kingdom, Jesus says, belongs to people like them. Most commentators take the point to be that the kingdom is received as a gift, not earned (10:15). From early times the scene has also been read about baptism: churches that baptize infants hear in "Do not stop them" a reason to bring children to Christ in baptism, and churches that baptize only believers note that Jesus blesses the children but does not baptize them. See the card on Matthew 19:14, which this site does not repeat here.

p: The Greek can mean "receive it as a child receives it" or "receive it as you would receive a child."
b: The phrase hōs paidion can be read two ways. Most take "child" as the subject: whoever does not receive the kingdom the way a child receives things, with open hands and trust. A smaller number take it as the object: whoever does not receive the kingdom as one receives a child, that is, as something small and easily overlooked (compare 9:37, "whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me"). The Plain English Translation follows the common reading but keeps the sense of welcome. Either way, the kingdom is not entered by status.

p: Mark uses a strong form of "bless" found only here in the New Testament.
b: Mark's verb, kateulogei, is the ordinary word for "bless" with a prefix that intensifies it, and the tense pictures him going from child to child. In Jewish custom elders laid hands on children to bless them (compare Jacob in Genesis 48:14–16). The disciples had tried to keep the children away; Jesus gives them more than was asked, for they had only been brought for him to touch.

a: a man ran up to him
p: Mark says only "a man." Matthew calls him young and Luke a ruler; the familiar title combines all three.
b: The well-known name "the rich young ruler" comes from putting the Gospels together. Mark says only "one" (a man) who ran up and knelt, and reveals at the end that he was rich (10:22). Matthew calls him "the young man" (Matthew 19:20, 22), and Luke "a ruler" (Luke 18:18). His running and kneeling show eagerness and respect: grown men of standing did not run in public. Mark's details of the man's approach and his face (10:22) are among the vivid touches that Matthew and Luke leave out.

p: A Jewish way to ask about the life of the age to come, the future share in God's world.
b: "Eternal life" is literally "the life of the age": the life of the age to come (10:30). The phrase first appears in Daniel 12:2, where some of the dead rise "to eternal life." "Inherit" comes from Israel's inheritance of the land and became a way to speak of a share in the world to come. Rabbis later asked the same question in the same terms, so the man's question is a Jewish one, asked sincerely. In Mark, entering eternal life, entering the kingdom of God (10:23–25) and being saved (10:26) are three ways of saying the same thing.

a: Why do you call me good?
t: Is Jesus denying that he is good?
p: Matthew reworded this question. Readers have argued over it since the 300s.
b: Matthew changes it to "Why are you asking me about the good?" (Matthew 19:17), which avoids any hint that Jesus is not good; Luke keeps Mark's form (Luke 18:19). Arius and his followers in the 300s used the verse to argue that the Son is less than God, and some Unitarians still read it that way. Most of the church fathers answered that Jesus is testing the man: if only God is good, then either the man must stop flattering him or he must see who Jesus really is (so Ambrose and others). Many modern scholars read it simply: Jesus, a devout Jew, turns praise away from himself to God, as Jewish teachers did. The words "except one: God" echo the Shema, "the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4), which returns in 12:29.

t: A commandment that is not in the Ten
p: "Do not defraud" is not one of the Ten Commandments. It may stand in for "do not covet," said to a rich man.
b: Jesus lists five of the Ten Commandments that deal with other people, but he adds "You must not cheat" (mē aposterēsēs, "do not defraud" or "do not withhold"), which is not among them. In the Greek Old Testament the same verb is used of withholding what is owed: a worker's wages (Malachi 3:5; compare the law of Deuteronomy 24:14–15) and a poor person's living ("do not defraud the poor of his living," Sirach 4:1). Many think it takes the place of "do not covet" and is aimed at a rich man, whose wealth may rest on wages held back (compare James 5:4). Matthew and Luke drop it, and some copyists of Mark did too (see the variant).
r: Exodus 20:12–16; Deuteronomy 5:16–20; Deuteronomy 24:14–15; Malachi 3:5; Sirach 4:1; James 5:4

a: fixed his eyes on him and loved him
p: Only Mark says this. It is the one place in the first three Gospels where Jesus is said to love someone.
b: Mark alone says that Jesus "looked at him" (the verb means a steady, searching look) "and loved him." Matthew and Luke both leave it out. In the first three Gospels this is the only time Jesus is said to love a particular person (John has several: John 11:5; 13:23). The order matters for the reading: the demand that follows, "sell whatever you have," comes out of love, not out of a wish to shame him. The man's sincerity (10:20) is not questioned.
orig: ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ἠγάπησεν αὐτόν (emblepsas autō ēgapēsen auton)

p: The verb is used of a sky that turns dark and overcast.
b: Stugnazō means to become gloomy. It is used of a darkening sky in Matthew 16:3 ("the sky is red and dark"), and in the Greek Old Testament of people appalled at a disaster (Ezekiel 27:35; Ezekiel 32:10). Mark pictures the man's face changing at Jesus' words before he turns away. He "left in grief": Mark does not say he never came back, and later readers have wondered. The reason given is plain: "He owned a great deal of property."

p: The only time in Mark that Jesus calls the disciples "children."
b: After a scene about little children (10:13–16), Jesus now calls his grown disciples tekna, "children," a teacher's word of affection. It also reminds them of what he has just said: only those who receive the kingdom like a child get into it (10:15). Riches make that kind of receiving hard.

p: A picture of the impossible. There is no evidence for a small city gate called "the needle's eye."
b: The camel was the largest animal in the land and the needle's eye the smallest opening, so the saying pictures something impossible, as 10:27 confirms. A popular explanation says "the needle's eye" was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall that a camel could pass through only by kneeling; no ancient source mentions such a gate, and the idea appears only in the Middle Ages. Another says the word should be kamilos, "rope," a reading found only in a few late manuscripts. The Babylonian Talmud uses a similar picture, an elephant through a needle's eye, for what no one could imagine (Bava Metzia 38b). See also the note on Matthew 19:24.
orig: κάμηλον διὰ τῆς τρυμαλιᾶς τῆς ῥαφίδος (kamēlon dia tēs trumalias tēs rhaphidos)

p: Wealth was often taken as a sign of God's blessing. If the rich cannot get in, who can?
b: In much of the Old Testament, wealth is a gift from God to the faithful (Deuteronomy 28:1–14; Job 42:10–12; Proverbs 10:22), even though the prophets attack the rich who oppress the poor (Amos 6:1–7). The rich could also give alms and offerings. So the disciples reason: if even the rich, who seem blessed and can do so much good, cannot get in, then no one can. Jesus agrees, and answers that salvation is God's work (10:27).

p: The words echo what the LORD said to Abraham about Sarah's son.
b: The saying recalls Genesis 18:14, where the LORD asks whether anything is too wonderful for him, and Job's confession (Job 42:2). In the Greek Old Testament the word adunatei, "be impossible," stands in Genesis 18:14, linking the birth of Isaac and the salvation of the rich. Mark uses the same Greek word, dunata, "possible," again in Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane (14:36). Compare also 9:23 and Luke 1:37.

a: because of me and because of the good news
p: Only Mark adds "the good news" here and in 8:35. It speaks to his readers, who suffered for the gospel.
b: Matthew has "because of my name" (Matthew 19:29) and Luke "because of the kingdom of God" (Luke 18:29). Mark, here and in 8:35, has "because of me and because of the good news." For Mark the "good news" is the message about Jesus that his church preaches (1:1; 13:10; 14:9). Readers who had lost homes and families for preaching it would hear the promise as theirs.
orig: ἕνεκεν ἐμοῦ καὶ ἕνεκεν τοῦ εὐαγγελίου (heneken emou kai heneken tou euangeliou)

a: a hundred times as much now
p: The new family of believers, said most of the fathers. Some modern preachers read it as money.
b: The list repeats the things left behind, but with "mothers" in the plural and no father: in the new family God alone is Father (compare 3:34–35 and Matthew 23:9). Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take the hundredfold to be the homes and families of the church, where a believer cast out by his family finds many brothers, sisters and mothers. Some preachers of the "prosperity gospel" have read it as a promise that money given to God returns a hundred times. Mark's own qualification, "along with persecutions," makes that reading hard to hold.

p: Only Mark adds these two words. They fit a church that knew suffering.
b: Matthew and Luke both leave out "with persecutions." In Mark the promise of a new family comes with a warning. Most scholars connect this with the situation of Mark's readers: if the Gospel was written in Rome, the persecution under Nero in AD 64, when Christians were burned and thrown to animals (Tacitus, Annals 15.44), was fresh; if in Syria or Galilee, the Jewish war of AD 66–70. Either way, the readers had found that following Jesus cost them families (13:12–13) and brought trials (13:9).

a: in the age that is coming
t: This age and the age to come
p: Jews spoke of two ages: this present one, and the age of God's rule that is coming.
b: Jesus divides time as many Jews of his day did: "this present time" and "the age that is coming." Rabbinic writings call them ha'olam hazzeh, "this world," and ha'olam habba', "the world to come." Eternal life, "the life of the age," belongs to the coming age (10:17), but Jesus promises that its family begins now.
orig: ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τῷ ἐρχομένῳ (en tō aiōni tō erchomenō)

a: Jesus was going on ahead of them
p: Mark pictures Jesus striding ahead to Jerusalem while the disciples follow in amazement and fear.
b: Mark alone gives this picture. Jesus walks in front, as a teacher led his pupils, and he is going knowingly toward death. Some following are "astounded" (the disciples) and others "afraid" (perhaps the wider group of pilgrims); the Greek may mean two groups or one. Fear and amazement in the face of Jesus run through Mark to its last line, "for they were afraid" (16:8). The scene also anticipates the promise that the risen Jesus "is going ahead of you into Galilee" (14:28; 16:7), the same verb.

p: Mark's word for the fate of John, of Jesus, and of Jesus' followers.
b: The verb paradidōmi means "hand over, betray." Mark uses it for John's arrest (1:14), for Judas (3:19; 14:10–11), for the Sanhedrin handing Jesus to Pilate (15:1) and Pilate handing him to be crucified (15:15), and for what will happen to the disciples (13:9, 11–12). The Greek of Isaiah 53 uses it of the servant: "the Lord handed him over for our sins" (Isaiah 53:6, Septuagint; compare Isaiah 53:12). Behind all the human hands, Mark suggests, is God's purpose (14:21).

p: Each step happens later in Mark: condemned (14:64), handed over (15:1), mocked and spat on (14:65; 15:19–20), whipped (15:15).
b: This is the most detailed of Jesus' three predictions of his death (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34), and every step comes true in Mark's passion story: the chief priests and scribes condemn him (14:64), hand him to the Gentiles (15:1), and he is spat on and mocked by the council's men (14:65) and by the soldiers (15:19–20), whipped (15:15) and killed (15:37). The details echo the suffering servant of Isaiah, who gave his back to those who struck him and did not hide his face from spitting (Isaiah 50:6). Critical scholars often think the prediction has been filled in from the events; others think Jesus foresaw what Rome did to troublemakers.

p: Mark's phrase means the same as "on the third day" in Matthew and Luke.
b: In all three predictions Mark says "after three days" (8:31; 9:31; 10:34); Matthew and Luke have "on the third day," and so do later copies of Mark here (see the variant). Jews counted part of a day as a day, so the two phrases meant the same thing: compare Esther 4:16 with Esther 5:1. Hosea 6:2, "on the third day he will raise us up," may lie behind the wording.

p: In Mark the brothers ask for themselves. In Matthew their mother asks.
b: Matthew has the mother of Zebedee's sons make the request (Matthew 20:20–21), though Jesus' answer is still to the two men. Luke leaves the scene out and places a dispute about greatness at the Last Supper (Luke 22:24–27). Many scholars see Matthew sparing the two apostles, a common pattern in how Matthew and Luke treat Mark's often unflattering picture of the Twelve. Right after Jesus' plainest prediction of his death, two of his closest friends ask for the best seats.

p: They picture Jesus on a throne. In Mark, the ones on his right and left turn out to be two bandits on crosses.
b: James and John imagine the Son of Man coming "in the glory of his Father" (8:38) and ask for the places of honor beside his throne. Mark's readers know where Jesus' "glory" will first be shown: on a cross, with "two bandits, one on his right and one on his left" (15:27). The same words, "right" and "left," bind the two scenes. The disciples who asked for the places will not be there.

p: In the prophets, God's cup is the cup of his anger, which the guilty must drink.
b: In the Old Testament a cup can stand for a person's lot, good (Psalm 23:5) or bad. The prophets speak of the cup of God's judgment: Jerusalem "drank from the LORD's hand the cup of his fury" (Isaiah 51:17; compare Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 25:15). In Gethsemane Jesus will pray for this cup to pass him by (14:36). Many interpreters take the cup to be the judgment Jesus bears for others, as 10:45 suggests; others take it more simply as his suffering and death. See also the note on Matthew 20:22.

a: be baptized with the baptism that I am being baptized with
p: Here "baptize" means to be plunged under or overwhelmed, a picture of Jesus' coming death.
b: Baptizō meant to dip or plunge, and in ordinary Greek it was used of a ship sunk or a person "drowned" in debt or troubles. The Psalms picture distress as waters closing over the head (Psalm 69:1–2; 42:7). Jesus speaks of his death as a baptism in Luke 12:50 too. Matthew leaves out the baptism saying here (Matthew 20:22). Later, Christians who died as martyrs before they could be baptized were said to have received "baptism of blood," a teaching that draws on this verse; the Catholic Church still teaches it (Catechism 1258).
orig: τὸ βάπτισμα ὃ ἐγὼ βαπτίζομαι (to baptisma ho egō baptizomai)

a: The cup I am drinking, you will drink
t: What happened to James and John
p: James was beheaded by Herod Agrippa I about AD 44. Accounts of John's death differ.
b: James, son of Zebedee, was the first of the Twelve to be killed: Herod Agrippa I had him executed with the sword (Acts 12:2), about AD 44. For John the evidence differs. Irenaeus, writing about AD 180, says John lived at Ephesus into the reign of Trajan (Against Heresies 3.3.4), and that became the common church tradition. But two late writers (Philip of Side in the 400s and George the Monk in the 800s) quote Papias as saying that John was killed by Jews, which some scholars take as evidence that both brothers died as martyrs. Many think that if this prediction had not come true for John, it would hardly have been kept.

a: the ones they have been prepared for
p: A passive verb that leaves God as the one who prepares. Matthew adds "by my Father."
b: Jewish speech often used the passive to speak of God's action without naming him. Matthew makes the subject clear: "the ones my Father has prepared them for" (Matthew 20:23). Jesus does not deny that there are places of honor; he denies that they are his to hand out on request. Mark's readers soon learn who occupied the places on his right and left (15:27).

a: those who are thought of as their rulers
p: Mark's wording quietly mocks the powers of the world: they only seem to rule.
b: Only Mark has hoi dokountes archein, literally "those who are reckoned to rule" or "those who seem to rule." The phrase can be neutral ("recognized rulers") or ironic: the real ruler is God, and the Roman emperor's power is only apparent. Paul uses the same verb for the leaders in Jerusalem, "those held in esteem as being something" (Galatians 2:6). For readers under Rome, the saying set the emperor's kind of power against the Son of Man's.

p: Mark's first use of "slave" (doulos). In the Roman world a slave was property, at the bottom of society.
b: This site renders doulos as "slave" and diakonos as "servant." Many English Bibles soften doulos to "servant," but in the Roman world a slave was owned property, with no rights, often working in a household, a field or a mine; slaves may have been a fifth or more of the population in Italy. A diakonos was one who served at table or ran errands, sometimes free. Jesus makes greatness mean taking the lowest place in both. In Mark's church, which likely had slaves and masters, the saying turned the social ladder upside down.

a: did not come to have people serve him
t: The Son of Man who serves
p: In Daniel 7 the Son of Man is given a kingdom and all peoples serve him. Jesus turns this around.
b: In Daniel 7:13–14, one "like a son of man" comes with the clouds and is given rule over all peoples, who "serve" him (the Greek of Daniel 7:14 uses words for serving and worship). Jesus, who calls himself the Son of Man, says he came for the opposite: to serve. The glory James and John asked for (10:37) will come, but by way of the cross. Mark has the Son of Man come in glory later (13:26; 14:62).

a: a ransom in place of many
p: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or a captive. "Many" echoes Isaiah 53.
b: Lutron was the payment that freed a slave or a prisoner of war, or redeemed a life that was forfeit (Exodus 21:30; 30:12). Anti means "in place of" or "in exchange for," and the Plain English Translation says "in place of," as at Matthew 20:28. Most English Bibles have "for many," which leaves open whether the death is a substitution or a benefit given on behalf of others; the traditions on the card below differ on just that. Many scholars hear Isaiah 53 in the verse: the servant gives his life as a guilt offering and "bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12; compare Isaiah 53:10–11). Others, such as C. K. Barrett and Morna Hooker, argued that the link to Isaiah 53 is weaker than it seems, and that the background is the suffering of the righteous and of the Son of Man's people in Daniel. "Many" in Hebrew idiom means "the multitude," not "some but not all"; compare "a ransom for all" (1 Timothy 2:6). How the death saves is the great question of Christian theology; see the card below, and the deep dive on Matthew 20.

p: Bartimaeus is the only person healed in Mark whose name is given.
b: "Bartimaeus" is Aramaic bar Timai, "son of Timai"; Mark gives the Greek translation first ("Timaeus' son"), unusually, before the Aramaic name. He is the only person healed in Mark who is named. Richard Bauckham argues that such names were kept because the people were known in the early church and could tell their own story. Matthew has two blind men, unnamed (Matthew 20:30), and Luke places the healing as Jesus enters Jericho (Luke 18:35); see the note on Matthew 20:30. Jericho, a palm oasis, was the last town before the climb of about 3,300 feet (1,000 meters) up to Jerusalem.

t: "Son of David" on the road to Jerusalem
p: The first time anyone in Mark calls Jesus Son of David, just before he enters David's city.
b: No one in Mark has called Jesus "Son of David" until now. The blind man, who cannot see, names him with the royal title of the Messiah, the promised king from David's line (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalms of Solomon 17:21). In the next scene the crowd hails "our father David's kingdom" (11:10), and in the temple Jesus asks how the Messiah can be only David's son (12:35–37). "Show me mercy" (eleēson me) became the church's prayer Kyrie eleison and, in the Orthodox Jesus Prayer, "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me."
r: 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalms of Solomon 17:21; 11:10; 12:35–37; Matthew 9:27; Matthew 20:30

p: A beggar's cloak was his bed and his alms cloth. He throws it away; the rich man could not leave his property.
b: For a poor man the outer cloak was his blanket at night (Exodus 22:26–27) and, for a beggar, the cloth spread out to catch coins. Bartimaeus throws it off and leaps up. Many readers set him beside the rich man of 10:17–22: the man with much property went away sad, and the beggar leaves his one possession to come to Jesus. Some early readers also saw in the cloak the old life thrown off at baptism.

p: An Aramaic form of "rabbi," "my master" or "my teacher." Mary Magdalene uses it in John 20:16.
b: Mark keeps the Aramaic word, as he often does (5:41; 7:34; 14:36; 15:34). Rabbouni is a fuller form of rabbi, perhaps more personal or respectful: "my master." John explains it as "Teacher" (John 20:16). Bartimaeus asks for what James and John did not: not a seat of honor but to see.

p: The healed man follows Jesus "on the road," the road to Jerusalem and the cross.
b: The man who has received his sight follows Jesus "on the road," the road up to Jerusalem and the cross. Here the road section that began with another blind man (8:22–26) comes to its end; for the design of the whole section, the word hodos, "road, way," and Christianity as "the Way," see the note on 8:27 and the deep dive on Mark 8. What is new here: others whom Jesus heals in Mark are sent home (5:19; 8:26), but Bartimaeus follows him; and "Your faith has saved you" uses the word for salvation (sesōken), as in 5:34, so the healing is also rescue.

a: Bethphage and Bethany by the Mount of Olives
t: Two villages on the Mount of Olives
p: Small villages on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, the last stop before Jerusalem.
b: Bethany lay about two miles (3 kilometers) east of Jerusalem on the road from Jericho (John 11:18); Bethphage ("house of unripe figs") was nearer the top of the Mount of Olives, though its exact site is uncertain. Coming from Jericho one reaches Bethany first, so Mark's order is loose. The Mount of Olives had a place in hope: Zechariah 14:4 says the LORD's feet will stand on it on the day he comes to fight for Jerusalem. Jesus spends his nights at Bethany during this last week (11:11–12; 14:3). See the note on Matthew 21:1.

p: In the Greek Old Testament a "colt" is a donkey's foal. Mark does not quote Zechariah 9:9, but readers knew it.
b: Pōlos means a young animal, and in ordinary Greek, standing alone, it often meant a young horse. In the Greek Old Testament, though, it is used of a donkey's foal (Genesis 49:11; Zechariah 9:9; Judges 10:4), and Matthew and John say plainly that it was a donkey (Matthew 21:2–7; John 12:14–15). The scholar Walter Bauer argued that Mark meant a horse; most disagree. Mark does not quote Zechariah 9:9, "your king is coming to you ... rides on a donkey, on a young male donkey," as Matthew and John do, but the scene acts it out. Genesis 49:11 may also be in view: the king from Judah ties "his donkey's colt to the choice vine" (Genesis 49:11).

a: one that no person has ever sat on yet
p: Animals for sacred use had never been worked. And no one else could ride a king's mount.
b: The law asked for animals "never put under a yoke" for some sacred uses (Numbers 19:2; Deuteronomy 21:3), and the Philistines sent back the ark on a cart pulled by cows that had never been yoked (1 Samuel 6:7). The Mishnah says that no one may ride the king's horse or sit on his throne (Mishnah Sanhedrin 2:5). So the unridden colt marks the ride as both holy and royal.

a: The Lord has need of it
p: "The Lord" may mean Jesus, God, or the colt's owner. Mark seldom calls Jesus "the Lord."
b: Ho kurios can mean "the master" or "the owner" as well as "the Lord." Some readers take it to mean the colt's owner, who is with Jesus, or God, who needs it. Most take it as Jesus speaking of himself, which would be striking in Mark, where the narrator never calls Jesus "the Lord" (except in the later ending, 16:19–20). The next sentence in the oldest manuscripts adds a promise to bring the colt back. In the Byzantine text the promise becomes a prediction that the owner will send it (see the variant).
orig: Ὁ κύριος αὐτοῦ χρείαν ἔχει (ho kurios autou chreian echei)

a: laid their own cloaks down on the road
p: Spreading cloaks was a way to greet a new king. Branches recall the welcome of the Maccabees.
b: When Jehu was proclaimed king of Israel, "each man grabbed his cloak and laid it down under him" (2 Kings 9:13). Waving branches greeted Simon the Maccabee when he entered the Citadel in Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 13:51) and the rededication of the temple (2 Maccabees 10:7). The crowd gives Jesus the welcome of a king or a deliverer. Mark's "greenery" (stibades) was leafy stuff cut in the fields, not specifically palms; only John mentions palm branches (John 12:13).

p: A Hebrew cry, "Save, please!" from Psalm 118, which pilgrims sang at the feasts.
b: Hosanna is the Hebrew hoshi'ah na, "Save, please!": "LORD, please, save us now!" (Psalm 118:25). The next verse, "Blessed is the one who comes in the LORD's name!" (Psalm 118:26), was a greeting to pilgrims arriving at the temple. Psalm 118 belongs to the Hallel (Psalms 113–118), sung at Passover and at the Feast of Booths. By Jesus' time "Hosanna" had become a shout of praise as well as a prayer. The crowd applies the psalm to Jesus. The Christian liturgy took up these words in the Sanctus: "Hosanna in the highest. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."
orig: Ὡσαννά (hōsanna), from Hebrew הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא (hoshi'ah na)

p: The crowd hopes Jesus will restore the kingdom of David. Mark's readers knew a different kind of kingdom.
b: Many Jews of the time hoped God would raise up a king from David's line to free Israel and restore his kingdom (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalms of Solomon 17:21–32). Mark alone has the crowd hail "our father David's kingdom." The welcome is real, but Mark has already shown what kind of king Jesus is: one who came to serve and give his life (10:45). In a few days, Pilate's soldiers will mock him as "King of the Jews" (15:18, 26). Readers in AD 70, when a revolt claiming God's help ended with the temple burned, could hear the cry with sorrow.

p: Perhaps "Save us, you who live in the highest heavens!" or simply praise from heaven too.
b: If hosanna means "save," then "in the highest" may address God in heaven: "Save us, you in the highest!" If, as is likely by this time, it had become a cry of praise, the phrase calls the heavens to join it, as in "up in the heights, praise him" (Psalm 148:1). Luke turns it into "glory in the highest" (Luke 19:38).
orig: Ὡσαννὰ ἐν τοῖς ὑψίστοις (hōsanna en tois hupsistois)

a: took a look around at everything
p: In Mark, Jesus' first visit to the temple is only a look. He acts the next day.
b: In Matthew and Luke Jesus goes straight to the temple and throws out the sellers on the day he arrives (Matthew 21:12; Luke 19:45). In Mark he only looks around and leaves, because it is late; the action comes the next day, wrapped in the story of the fig tree. Many readers hear Malachi 3:1–2, where the Lord "will suddenly come to his temple" and asks "who can endure the day of his coming?" Mark's slower order gives three days to the week's opening (11:1, 12, 20), and many scholars think it is the older one.

a: It was not the time for figs
t: Why curse a tree when it was not fig season?
p: Mark's comment shows the act is a sign, not a fit of hunger. The tree stands for the temple.
b: Fig trees around Jerusalem put out leaves in spring; the main crop ripens in late summer. Readers have long asked why Jesus would curse a tree for not bearing fruit out of season. Bertrand Russell cited it as a reason he could not admire Jesus' character. Most commentators answer that Mark tells the story as a prophetic sign, like the prophets' acted-out messages (Jeremiah 13:1–11; 19:1–13), and that his remark about the season is a signal not to read it as an ordinary event. The prophets used the fig tree for Israel: God looks for figs and finds none (Jeremiah 8:13; Micah 7:1; Hosea 9:10, 16). Some add that leaves raised a hope of the small early figs that form before the leaves, so a leafy tree with none was barren. Because Mark wraps the fig tree around the temple scene (11:12–25), most scholars take the withered tree as a picture of judgment on the temple, as William Telford argued in detail. See also the note on Matthew 21:19.
r: Jeremiah 8:13; Micah 7:1; Hosea 9:10; Hosea 9:16; Joel 1:7; Luke 13:6–9; Matthew 21:18–19

p: The fig tree story is split in two, with the temple scene in the middle. Each half explains the other.
b: Mark often starts one story, interrupts it with another, and then finishes the first (3:20–35; 5:21–43; 6:7–30; 14:1–11; 14:54–72). Here the cursed tree (11:12–14) and the withered tree (11:20–25) frame Jesus' action in the temple (11:15–19). The disciples "were listening": they will be witnesses of what the curse means. Matthew tells the fig tree story in one piece, after the temple scene (Matthew 21:18–22), and the link is less clear.

p: Money changers turned pilgrims' coins into the silver used for the temple tax; dove sellers sold the poor's offerings.
b: Every Jewish man paid a half-shekel each year to the temple (Exodus 30:13), and it had to be paid in Tyrian silver; the Mishnah says the changers set up their tables in the temple three weeks before Passover (Mishnah Shekalim 1:3). Doves were the offering of the poor and of women after childbirth (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8). The trade took place in the great outer court built by Herod, open to Gentiles, probably in or near the Royal Portico along its southern side. The trade served the worship the Law required, so Jesus' action was not simply against cheating. What it meant is debated: see the chapter page. See also the note on Matthew 21:12.

a: He would not let anyone carry a container through the temple
p: Only Mark has this. Jewish rules also forbade using the Temple Mount as a shortcut.
b: The word translated "container" (skeuos) means any vessel or piece of equipment. Some think Jesus stopped people carrying goods through the courts as a shortcut, which the Mishnah also forbids: no one may enter the Temple Mount with staff, sandals or wallet, or make it a shortcut (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5). Others think he stopped the carrying of vessels used for the temple's own business, halting its worship for a moment, which would make the act a sign of the end of the sacrifices. Zechariah 14:21 pictures a day when every pot in Jerusalem is holy and "there will no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD."

a: a house of prayer for all the nations
p: Only Mark keeps the end of Isaiah 56:7. The market filled the one court where Gentiles could pray.
b: Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7: "for my house will be called a house of prayer for all the peoples" (Isaiah 56:7). Matthew and Luke leave out the last words (Matthew 21:13; Luke 19:46); Mark keeps them. In Isaiah the promise is for foreigners and eunuchs who join themselves to the LORD (Isaiah 56:3–8). The trading took place in the outer court, the only part of the temple Gentiles could enter; warning stones (two have been found) threatened death to any foreigner who went further. Mark's mostly Gentile readers would have noticed the words. Mark's Greek follows the Septuagint, "nations," where the Hebrew has "peoples."

p: From Jeremiah 7:11. A bandits' cave is where robbers hide between raids, not where they rob.
b: Jesus joins Isaiah to Jeremiah 7:11, part of Jeremiah's speech in the temple gate warning that the temple would not protect people who did wrong and then came to it feeling safe; it would be destroyed like Shiloh (Jeremiah 7:1–15). A cave for bandits is a hideout. So the charge may be less about cheating in the market than about trusting the temple while doing injustice. The word lēstēs, "bandit," was also used by Josephus for the armed rebels who later made the temple their stronghold in the war of 66–70 (Jewish War 4.151–157); some scholars think Mark's readers heard that too. Jesus himself will be crucified between two lēstai (15:27).

a: they tried to find how they might do away with him
p: Until now the plot against Jesus came from Galilean Pharisees and Herodians (3:6). Now the chief priests join.
b: The chief priests were the high priest and the leading priestly families who ran the temple under the Roman governor; the scribes were the experts in the law. They had the means to act. In 3:6 Pharisees and Herodians plotted against Jesus in Galilee; from here on in Mark, the Jerusalem priesthood leads, and the Pharisees all but disappear after 12:13. Sanders argued that an action against the temple, the center of Jewish worship and of Roman order in Judea, is the most likely immediate cause of Jesus' arrest.

p: Not just the leaves: the whole tree is dead. The prophets used the picture for judgment.
b: "From the roots" means the tree is wholly dead. Job's friend pictures the wicked so: "Underneath, his roots go dry" (Job 18:16), and Hosea says of Ephraim, "Their root has withered; fruit they will not make" (Hosea 9:16). Mark's readers, if they wrote or read after AD 70, had seen the temple left in ruins; Jesus foretells it in 13:2.

p: The Greek says "faith of God." Almost all take it as faith in God.
b: The Greek is pistin theou, "faith of God," which could mean faith that has God as its object ("faith in God") or the faith that God gives or has. Nearly all translations and commentators read "faith in God." Some teachers in the Word of Faith movement, such as Kenneth Hagin, have read it as "have the God kind of faith," faith that speaks things into being; most scholars find no support for that in the grammar. A few manuscripts read "If you have faith in God" (see the variant).

p: "Moving mountains" was a Jewish saying for doing the impossible. On the road to Jerusalem, "this mountain" may be the temple mount.
b: Jewish teachers later called a brilliant scholar an "uprooter of mountains" (Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 64a), and Paul uses the picture of faith to "move mountains" (1 Corinthians 13:2). So Jesus may simply mean that nothing is too hard for faith in God. But Jesus speaks between the Mount of Olives and the temple mount, after acting against the temple, and "this mountain" may be pointed. Zechariah 14:4 pictures the Mount of Olives split in two on the day of the LORD. Some scholars, among them Telford, read the saying as part of the fig tree sign: the temple mount, like the fig tree, will be removed, and prayer will no longer need it. See also the note on Matthew 21:21.

a: whenever you are standing in prayer
p: Jews usually stood to pray. The saying is close to the forgiveness line of the Lord's Prayer.
b: Standing was the ordinary posture of Jewish prayer (1 Samuel 1:26; 1 Kings 8:22; Luke 18:11–13); the main synagogue prayer, the Eighteen Blessings, is still called the Amidah, "the Standing." Mark has no Lord's Prayer, but this saying shares its words: "your Father who is in heaven" (only here in Mark) and the link between forgiving others and being forgiven (Matthew 6:12, 14–15). After the temple scene, Jesus speaks of prayer that does not depend on the temple.
r: 1 Samuel 1:26; 1 Kings 8:22; Luke 18:11–13; Matthew 6:12; Matthew 6:14–15; Matthew 18:35

a: the chief priests, the scribes and the elders
t: The three groups of the council
p: The same three groups Jesus named in his first prediction of his death (8:31).
b: These were the leaders who made up the Sanhedrin, the high council in Jerusalem: the chief priests, the experts in the law, and the elders, heads of leading lay families. Jesus had named exactly these three groups when he first foretold that he would be rejected (8:31), and they will condemn him (14:43, 53; 15:1). Their question about authority was a fair one from their side: they were responsible for the temple, and Jesus had just disrupted it without any office.

a: was it from heaven, or from human beings?
p: "Heaven" here means God. Jews often used it to avoid saying God's name.
b: "From heaven" means "from God," a reverent Jewish way of speaking (compare Matthew's "kingdom of heaven," and the prodigal son's "I have sinned against heaven," Luke 15:18). Jesus' counter-question was a normal way to argue in Jewish debate, and it links his authority to John's. If John came from God, so did the one John announced (1:7–8). See the note on Matthew 21:25.

a: But suppose we say, 'From human beings'...
p: The leaders break off, and Mark finishes the thought for them: they were afraid of the crowd.
b: In the Greek the leaders' sentence stops short, and Mark's narration takes over: "They were afraid of the crowd." The broken grammar pictures men who dare not finish what they are thinking. Matthew and Luke tidy it into a full sentence (Matthew 21:26; Luke 20:6).
orig: ἀλλὰ εἴπωμεν· Ἐξ ἀνθρώπων;— (alla eipōmen: ex anthrōpōn?)

p: The parable starts from Isaiah's song of the vineyard, which ancient Jewish readers linked to the temple.
b: The hedge, the winepress and the tower come from Isaiah 5:1–2: "In the middle of it he built a tower; he even carved a wine vat out of the rock in it" (Isaiah 5:2), where the vineyard is "the house of Israel" (Isaiah 5:7). In Isaiah the vineyard itself fails; in Jesus' parable the vineyard is fine and the tenants are at fault. Ancient Jewish readers connected the song with the temple: the Aramaic Targum of Isaiah turns the tower into the sanctuary and the wine vat into the altar, and a Qumran fragment (4Q500) links the vineyard, its winepress and the temple. Jesus tells the parable in the temple courts to the temple's leaders. See also the note on Matthew 21:33.

a: leased it out to farmers and left the country
p: Rich owners who lived far away leased their land to tenant farmers. Quarrels and violence were common.
b: Large estates owned by people living elsewhere were common in Galilee and Judea, and the owners leased them to tenants for a share of the crop. A new vineyard gave no fruit for its first years (Leviticus 19:23–25), so the owner's first claim came later. Papyri from Egypt, including the archive of Zenon (200s BC), which deals with an estate in Galilee, record tenants who refused to pay and agents who were beaten. John Kloppenborg's study of these papyri shows the parable's story was realistic. Hearers who were themselves tenants might at first have sided with the farmers.

a: he sent a slave to the farmers
p: "My servants the prophets": the Old Testament often calls the prophets God's servants.
b: The Old Testament often calls the prophets God's "servants" (the Greek uses douloi, "slaves"): "I sent you all my servants the prophets, sending them again and again" is Jeremiah's refrain (Jeremiah 7:25; 25:4; compare Amos 3:7). Their mistreatment is a theme of 2 Chronicles 36:15–16 and Nehemiah 9:26. Hearers would naturally take the slaves for the prophets, and the son for someone greater.
r: Jeremiah 7:25; Jeremiah 25:4; Amos 3:7; 2 Chronicles 36:15–16; Nehemiah 9:26; Matthew 23:34–37

p: The same words as the voice at Jesus' baptism and transfiguration (1:11; 9:7).
b: God's voice called Jesus "my dearly loved Son" at his baptism (1:11) and on the mountain (9:7); now Jesus uses the same words of the son in the parable, close to saying openly who he is. The phrase also recalls Abraham's son: "Take your son, please, your only one, whom you love" (Genesis 22:2), where the Greek has "your beloved son." "Last of all" marks the son as the final messenger: after him there will be no other.

p: The tenants hope to keep the land. Some think they assumed the owner was dead.
b: Joachim Jeremias suggested that the farmers took the son's arrival to mean the owner had died, so that killing the heir would leave the property ownerless and theirs by possession. Others say no legal theory is needed: the story is about greed and rebellion, and it need not be realistic at this point. The words "Come on, let us kill him" echo Joseph's brothers: "Come on now, let's kill him" (Genesis 37:20).

a: They grabbed him and killed him, and cast him outside the vineyard
p: In Mark the son is killed first and his body thrown out unburied. Matthew and Luke reverse the order.
b: Mark's order means the body was thrown out without burial, a final dishonor. Matthew and Luke have the son thrown out of the vineyard first and then killed (Matthew 21:39; Luke 20:15), which matches Jesus' death outside the city wall (John 19:17; Hebrews 13:12). Many scholars see the later Gospels shaping the parable to the passion; Mark's order is probably the earlier.
orig: ἀπέκτειναν αὐτόν, καὶ ἐξέβαλον αὐτόν (apekteinan auton, kai exebalon auton)

p: Mark says the parable was aimed at the leaders (12:12). Later Christians often read it as God rejecting the Jewish people.
b: In Mark the farmers are the temple leaders, who "could tell the parable was aimed at them" (12:12); the vineyard, Israel, is not destroyed but given to new caretakers. Who they are is debated: the Twelve, as new leaders of Israel; the church of Jews and Gentiles; or simply God's choice. For many centuries Christians read the parable as God's rejection of the Jewish people as a whole, and it was used to justify contempt for Jews. Many scholars today, Jewish and Christian, point out that Mark's text aims it at the rulers in Jerusalem, who did lose their place when the temple fell in AD 70. See the card on Matthew 21:43, where Matthew adds "given to a nation that yields its fruit."

a: A stone that the builders threw out
p: Psalm 118:22–23. In Hebrew, "son" (ben) and "stone" (eben) sound alike.
b: Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22–23, from the same Hallel psalm the crowd had sung (11:9): "A stone that the builders threw out has become the head of the corner" (Psalm 118:22). The early church used the verse often (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:4–7). Many scholars note a wordplay that works in Hebrew: ben, "son," and 'eben, "stone." The rejected son of the parable is the rejected stone of the psalm, and the "builders" are the leaders who should have known. The head of the corner was either the cornerstone or the capstone over an arch.
orig: Λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες (lithon hon apedokimasan hoi oikodomountes)

p: A Roman tax on every person in Judea, begun in AD 6. Mark uses the Latin word, census.
b: The kēnsos (Latin census) was a yearly tax paid by each adult in Judea after it became a Roman province in AD 6. Its start provoked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean, who taught that paying it meant accepting slavery under human masters instead of God (Josephus, Jewish War 2.118; Antiquities 18.1–10). So the question was a trap: "yes" would anger the crowd who hated the tax; "no" would be treason that the Herodians could report. Mark uses the Latin word, one of several Latin terms in his Gospel (15:39 kenturiōn, 12:42 kodrantēs), which many take as a sign that he wrote for readers in the Roman West. See also the note on Matthew 22:17.

a: Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God
p: The coin bears Caesar's image; people bear God's image. What then belongs to Caesar?
b: The denarius of Tiberius carried his portrait and called him son of the divine Augustus. "Pay back" (apodote) means giving what is owed: Caesar may have back his coin. But the saying sets a second debt beside it, and Jewish hearers knew whose image people bear (Genesis 1:27). Tertullian made that point: give Caesar his image on the coin, and God his image in you (On Idolatry 15). Readers have drawn very different conclusions about church and state from the verse; see the card and the deep dive on Matthew 22.

p: The priestly upper class of Jerusalem. They denied the resurrection. This is their only appearance in Mark.
b: The Sadducees were a party of the priestly and wealthy families of Jerusalem, many of them connected to the high priesthood. Josephus says they rejected the traditions of the Pharisees and kept only the written laws (Antiquities 13.297), and that they denied life after death and its rewards and punishments (Jewish War 2.165; Antiquities 18.16). Acts says they denied resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). Resurrection is taught most clearly in the Hebrew Bible in Daniel 12:2 (compare Isaiah 26:19), both outside the five books of Moses, so the Sadducees could ask where the Torah teaches it. The party disappears from history after the temple fell in AD 70.
r: Acts 23:6–8; Acts 4:1–2; Daniel 12:2; Isaiah 26:19; Matthew 22:23; Luke 20:27

p: The law of Deuteronomy 25:5–6: if a man died childless, his brother married the widow to give him an heir.
b: The Sadducees cite Deuteronomy 25:5–6: "Her husband's brother is to go in to her and take her as his wife, and do a brother-in-law's duty to her" (Deuteronomy 25:5), so that the first son would carry on the dead man's name. Compare Genesis 38:8 and the story of Ruth. Their story of seven brothers may borrow from Tobit, where Sarah had been given to seven husbands who all died (Tobit 3:8). The question mocks the resurrection: if the dead rise, the law of Moses itself makes a nonsense of it. See also the note on Matthew 22:24.

p: In the main Jewish prayer, the blessing about raising the dead is called "the Powers."
b: Jesus charges the Sadducees with not knowing two things: the Scriptures (answered in 12:26–27) and God's power (answered in 12:25). The second blessing of the Eighteen Blessings, the Jewish prayer said daily, praises God as mighty, "who gives life to the dead," and the Mishnah calls it the blessing of "the resurrection of the dead" (Mishnah Berakhot 5:2). The Mishnah also says that whoever denies that the resurrection of the dead is taught in the Torah has no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). On this question Jesus stands with the Pharisees.

a: They are like angels in the heavens
p: The raised will not marry, since they will not die. Jewish writings also said the righteous would be like angels.
b: Marriage in Jewish thought served to carry on life through children (the very point of the brother-in-law's duty). In the resurrection there is no more death (Luke 20:36), so no need of heirs. Jewish apocalyptic writings also say the righteous will shine like the stars or be like the angels (Daniel 12:3; 1 Enoch 104:4–6; 2 Baruch 51:10). There is an edge here: the Sadducees, Acts says, denied angels too (Acts 23:8). Jesus does not say the raised become angels, only that they are like them in this. Churches differ on whether marriage continues; see the card on Matthew 22:30.
r: Luke 20:34–36; Daniel 12:3; 1 Enoch 104:4–6; 2 Baruch 51:10; Acts 23:8; Matthew 22:30

p: Before chapters and verses, a passage was named by its subject: "at the bush" means Exodus 3.
b: The Greek epi tou batou means "in the passage about the bush." Scripture had no chapter numbers, so passages were known by a key word (compare Romans 11:2, "in Elijah"). The quotation is Exodus 3:6, "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob" (Exodus 3:6). Jesus' argument is that God still calls himself their God long after they died, and God is not God of the dead: so they must live to him. The rabbis also looked for the resurrection in the Torah, with other verses (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 90b). See the note on Matthew 22:32.

p: In Mark this scribe is friendly and Jesus praises him. Matthew makes his question a test.
b: Matthew turns the scribe into a lawyer who asks "as a test" (Matthew 22:35), and Luke has a lawyer "testing" him in another setting (Luke 10:25). In Mark the scribe has heard Jesus answer well, asks honestly, agrees warmly, and is told he is "not far from the kingdom of God" (12:34). Mark's picture of the scribes is mostly hostile (12:38–40), so this scene matters: it shows Jesus and a teacher of the law in agreement on the heart of the Torah. Jewish scholars note that the conversation is entirely at home in Judaism.

a: Listen, Israel: The Lord is our God. The Lord is one.
p: Only Mark has Jesus quote the opening line of the Shema, the creed that Jews recited morning and evening.
b: Deuteronomy 6:4–5, with Deuteronomy 11:13–21 and Numbers 15:37–41, is the Shema, named for its first word, "Listen!" Jews recited it every morning and evening (Mishnah Berakhot 1:1–4), as they still do. This site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4); in the Greek the divine name is "Lord," so the New Testament has "the Lord," and the line can also be read "the Lord our God, the Lord is one." Matthew and Luke leave out this opening and quote only the command to love (Matthew 22:37). Mark's Jesus begins where every Jew began. For Gentile readers in Mark's church, who had come from many gods, the line was the first thing to learn.

p: Deuteronomy has three terms; Mark's Jesus has four, adding "mind."
b: The Hebrew of Deuteronomy 6:5 has heart, being (nefesh) and strength (me'od). Copies of the Greek Old Testament differ, some reading "mind" (dianoia) for "heart." Mark keeps both, giving four: heart, being, mind, strength; Matthew has three, with "mind" for "strength" (Matthew 22:37), and the scribe in 12:33 has his own three. The point is the same in every form: love God with the whole self. "Being" translates psuchē, the life or self, as this site renders nefesh in Deuteronomy.
orig: ἐξ ὅλης τῆς διανοίας σου (ex holēs tēs dianoias sou)

a: You are to love your neighbor as yourself
p: Leviticus 19:18. Jewish writings before Jesus had also joined love of God and love of neighbor.
b: Jesus adds Leviticus 19:18, "You are to love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18). Rabbi Akiva later called this verse "a great principle of the Torah" (Sifra on Leviticus 19:18), and Hillel summed up the Torah in its negative form (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a). The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs join the two loves: "love the Lord and your neighbor" (Testament of Issachar 5:2; Testament of Dan 5:3), and Philo calls piety toward God and justice toward people the two chief heads of the law (On the Special Laws 2.63). Jesus' pairing is not new in Judaism, but he ranks these two above all others. See the note on Matthew 22:39.
r: Leviticus 19:18; Leviticus 19:34; Romans 13:9; Galatians 5:14; James 2:8; Matthew 22:39

a: more than all the burnt offerings and sacrifices
p: The scribe echoes the prophets: "listening is better than sacrifice." Said in the temple, it carries weight.
b: The scribe's words echo Samuel, "listening is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22), Hosea 6:6 and Proverbs 21:3. Neither he nor the prophets reject sacrifice; they rank it below love and obedience. Said in the temple courts, just after Jesus' action against the temple trade, it has extra point. After the temple was destroyed in AD 70, Jewish teachers drew the same comfort from the prophets: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai is said to have told a grieving disciple that acts of loving-kindness atone as the sacrifices did, citing Hosea 6:6 (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4).
r: 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Proverbs 21:3; Micah 6:6–8; Psalm 51:16–17; Matthew 9:13

a: You are not far from the kingdom of God
p: Praise, or a gentle invitation to take the last step? Mark leaves it open.
b: Only this scribe, of all Jesus' questioners in Mark, is praised. "Not far" can be heard as a warm compliment or as a call: he is near, but not yet in. Christian readers have often supplied the missing step as following Jesus himself (compare 10:21). Mark does not say what the scribe did next. The scene closes the series of questions in the temple (11:27–12:34): "no one dared to question him any longer."

p: The scribes taught that the Messiah would be a son of David. Jesus does not deny it but asks what it means.
b: Expecting a Messiah from David's line rests on God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:12–16) and the prophets (Isaiah 11:1–10; Jeremiah 23:5). The Psalms of Solomon, written in the first century BC, pray, "raise up for them their king, the son of David" (Psalms of Solomon 17:21). Jesus has just been hailed as Son of David (10:47–48; 11:10). His question in the temple does not reject the title; it asks how David could call his own descendant "Lord."
r: 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1–10; Jeremiah 23:5; Psalms of Solomon 17:21; 10:47; 11:10; Matthew 22:42

a: The Lord said to my Lord
p: The verse the New Testament quotes more than any other. In Hebrew the first "Lord" is God's name; the second is "my lord."
b: Psalm 110:1 reads in the Hebrew, "The LORD declares to my lord" (Psalm 110:1): YHWH speaks to adoni, "my lord," a title for a king. The Greek has kurios for both. Jesus, like his hearers, takes David as the speaker, so David calls the Messiah his lord. Many modern scholars think the psalm was first sung by a court poet about the king, so that "my lord" was the king himself. Later rabbinic readings applied it to Abraham (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 32b) or to the Messiah. The New Testament quotes or echoes this verse more than any other Old Testament verse (Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13), and Jesus uses it again at his trial (14:62).

a: So in what sense is he his son?
t: Is Jesus denying he is David's son?
p: Most read it as "more than David's son." A few scholars think Jesus rejected the title.
b: Most interpreters, ancient and modern, read the riddle as saying that the Messiah is David's son but also more: David's Lord, seated at God's right hand. Paul puts both together (Romans 1:3–4). A minority of scholars have argued that Jesus, or Mark, meant to deny that the Messiah must come from David's line, perhaps because Jesus' own descent was questioned; Matthew and Luke, with their genealogies, clearly do not read it that way. The crowd's delight shows Jesus winning the contest in the temple.

a: Be on guard against the scribes who like to go about in long robes
p: The Greek can mean "the scribes, who like..." (all of them) or "the scribes who like..." (some of them).
b: The participle phrase can describe the scribes as a group or pick out those who behave this way. The Plain English Translation reads it as "the scribes who like...": Mark has just shown a scribe whom Jesus praised (12:28–34). Jesus' charges are vanity (robes, greetings, best seats) and greed under cover of piety (12:40). Jewish writings also criticize such conduct among teachers (for example, the warnings against using the Torah for one's own honor in Mishnah Avot 4:5). Matthew expands this short warning into a long chapter of woes (Matthew 23).

p: Perhaps managing widows' estates for profit, or living off their gifts. The Law protected widows.
b: The Law and the prophets demanded care for widows: "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly" (Exodus 22:22; compare Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 10:1–2). How scribes "ate up" their houses is not explained. Suggestions include acting as trustees of widows' property and taking large fees, taking advantage of their hospitality, or urging gifts to the temple beyond their means. The next scene shows a widow giving her whole living (12:41–44). "A heavier sentence" assumes that those who teach God's law are judged more strictly (compare James 3:1). See the variant at Matthew 23:14, which comes from this verse.
r: Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 10:1–2; Malachi 3:5; James 3:1; Luke 20:47; Matthew 23:14

p: Thirteen trumpet-shaped chests stood in the temple courts for offerings.
b: The Mishnah describes thirteen chests shaped like rams' horns (shofarot) in the temple, each marked for a different kind of offering (Mishnah Shekalim 6:1, 5); they stood probably in the Court of the Women, which both men and women could enter. Givers could be watched as they dropped their coins in, and some say the size of a gift could be heard. Mark's word for the money, chalkos, literally means "copper" or "bronze," but it was the ordinary word for money in small coins, so the Plain English Translation says "money."

a: two small coins called lepta, which add up to a quadrans
p: The lepton was the smallest coin in use. Mark explains it by a Roman coin, the quadrans.
b: The lepton (plural lepta) was the smallest bronze coin in Judea, the kind struck by the Hasmonean kings and later the Roman governors. Mark tells his readers its value in Roman money: two lepta made a quadrans (Greek kodrantēs), a quarter of the Roman as and a sixty-fourth of a denarius, a day's wage. Many scholars take the explanation as a clue that Mark wrote for readers who knew Roman coins, perhaps in Rome; others reply that the quadrans was known in the East as a unit of value even where it did not circulate. The widow gave two coins: she could have kept one.
orig: λεπτὰ δύο, ὅ ἐστιν κοδράντης (lepta duo, ho estin kodrantēs)

p: Jesus may praise her giving, or lament a system that took a poor widow's last coins. Readers differ.
b: The traditional reading, found in most sermons from the church fathers on, takes Jesus to praise the widow: God measures a gift by what it costs, and she gave more than all. Addison Wright argued in 1982 that the context points the other way: Jesus has just condemned scribes who "eat up widows' houses" (12:40), and he next foretells that the temple will be torn down (13:1–2). Read so, he laments that a poor widow was led to give "her whole living" to an institution about to fall. Many readers hold both: Jesus honors her devotion and condemns those who profit from it. "Her whole living" (holon ton bion) can also mean "her whole life," and some note that Jesus is about to give his whole life too.
orig: ὅλον τὸν βίον αὐτῆς (holon ton bion autēs)
